Pruritus is an early and prominent symptom in intrahepatic cholestasis (e.g., primary biliary cholangitis — PBC), often preceding significant jaundice; PBC is the most common autoimmune cholestatic disorder in middle-aged women and fits the chronicity (2 months). Obstructive causes like choledocholithiasis are highly plausible given acute-onset jaundice and pruritus, though pain is absent — but up to 30% of CBD stones are painless ('silent stones'). Autoimmune hepatitis can present with cholestasis (AIH-PSC or AIH-cholestatic overlap), especially with fatigue and pruritus, though jaundice is usually less prominent early. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is less likely without IBD history or male predominance, but remains in differential due to overlapping serology and imaging findings. Hepatocellular carcinoma is lower probability but must be considered in patients with risk factors (e.g., cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, alcohol) causing biliary obstruction or intrahepatic cholestasis; however, absence of known risk factors or weight loss lowers confidence. Extrahepatic malignancies (e.g., pancreatic CA) were excluded from top 5 as they typically cause painless jaundice but less prominent pruritus early and usually lack isolated fatigue/itch without other GI symptoms — though not impossible, confidence <0.6."}

PBC is the most likely diagnosis given the chronicity (2 months), absence of acute pain/fever (making acute obstruction less likely), and classic phenotype. Common bile duct stone remains highly plausible despite lack of reported biliary colic (up to 30% of patients with choledocholithiasis may be asymptomatic or have atypical presentations); it explains all symptoms and is a critical diagnosis to rule out urgently. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is less common, often associated with IBD, and typically has a more variable course—but fits the cholestatic profile. Cholestatic DILI is plausible if the patient recently started medications (e.g., antibiotics, antifungals, NSAIDs), but no drug history was provided; thus assigned lower confidence. Acute viral hepatitis (e.g., HBV, HAV) is less likely given absence of flu-like symptoms, anorexia, or dark urine in the prompt, and the prominence of pruritus over other constitutional symptoms."}

Pruritus is an early and prominent symptom in cholestatic disorders due to accumulation of bile acids; fatigue is common and often disproportionate; scleral icterus confirms hyperbilirubinemia. The absence of reported colicky RUQ pain or fever/chills makes acute cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis less likely, though partial or intermittent obstruction (e.g., choledocholithiasis) remains plausible—especially given the subacute onset over two months and lack of overt acute features. Pale stools were not confirmed but are highly suggestive if present; their absence lowers—but does not exclude—obstructive causes. Primary biliary cholangitis is the most common adult autoimmune cholestatic disease, typically presenting in middle-aged women with pruritus and fatigue preceding jaundice; AMA positivity would support this. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is also cholestatic and pruritic but more commonly associated with IBD and multifocal strictures. Cholangiocarcinoma must be considered in any unexplained cholestasis, particularly with progressive symptoms and no clear autoimmune serology. Autoimmune hepatitis can present with cholestasis (AIH-PSC overlap or severe interface hepatitis), though pruritus is less dominant than in pure cholestatic diseases. Viral hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease are less likely given the prominence of pruritus and absence of systemic viral symptoms or alcohol history."}
